# Flow: Auto Codex - Delegates to `/flow-auto`, Which Now Carries the Stage

**This command no longer adds a stage. `/flow-auto` does the whole thing.**

Counter-model review - a second model reading the branch before the PR exists -
moved into `/flow-auto` Step 6 in issue #934. This command remains as a working
entry point that delegates there, so nothing driving on it breaks.

## What to do

Run `/flow-auto` with the same arguments. That is the entire behaviour:

```
/flow-auto <ISSUE> [PROJECT]
```

Everything this command used to describe - the review, its triage, the bounded
second pass, the summary appended to the PR body - is in `/flow-auto` Step 6
item 2, plus a receipt this command never wrote. Load
`.claude/commands/flow/auto.md` and execute it exactly. Do NOT re-derive a
lifecycle from this file: it no longer contains one.

Report at the start:

```
Flow Auto Codex: delegating to /flow-auto (issue #934 folded the
counter-model stage into the default lifecycle; this command is an alias).
```

`--yes` / `--auto-approve` remain recognized and refused. The ELI5 approval
pause has no bypass (issue #775), and delegation does not create one.

## Why this command still exists

**It is a live wave driver.** The flow-wave registry records a `driver` per role,
and roles declare `driver=flow:auto_codex`. Deleting the command while sessions
are running on it removes the lifecycle command those sessions are executing -
including, in the wave where this change was made, the session implementing the
removal. That is not a merge conflict; it is three in-flight PRs losing their
driver mid-run.

Issue #934 asks for this command to be retired as a separate command. The
separate *stage* is retired here and now - that was the substance. The command
name outlives it by exactly as long as something is driving on it.

## RETIREMENT TRIGGER (issue #934, and #936's rule about two-sided changes)

Delete this file, and `codex/skills/flow-auto_codex/`, when:

> **no live role in any wave declares `driver=flow:auto_codex`.**

Checkable by reading, not by waiting for somebody to report. **But an empty
grep is not the condition**, and the obvious one-liner gets this wrong in two
directions at once:

- a registry that cannot be read, or a helper that is not installed, produces
  no matching output - and that is UNKNOWN, not "nobody is using it";
- `list` renders RELEASED and stale roles with their drivers too, so a
  substring scan counts sessions that ended months ago and blocks the
  retirement forever. `worker-A` in the wave that wrote this is exactly that
  case: `liveness: released`, `driver: flow:auto_codex`.

Per wave, against the registry's real shape - a JSON object keyed by role name,
carrying `liveness` and an exact `driver`, followed by `FLOW_WAVE_*` contract
lines that are not part of the JSON:

```bash
raw=$(~/.claude/scripts/flow-wave-registry.sh list --wave "$WAVE" --json 2>/dev/null) || {
    echo "RETIREMENT: unknown - the registry could not be enumerated"; exit 3; }

# The JSON is an object keyed by ROLE NAME, followed by FLOW_WAVE_* contract
# lines that are not part of it. Alongside the roles sit METADATA keys -
# `wave_policy` (#699) and `unregistered_claims` (#687), the latter an ARRAY -
# so a filter that drops only `wave_policy` then asks an array for `.liveness`
# and the whole query dies, reporting `unknown` on a roster that was perfectly
# readable.
roster=$(printf '%s' "$raw" | sed '/^FLOW_WAVE/,$d' | jq -c '
    to_entries
    | map(select(.key | IN("wave_policy", "unregistered_claims", "merge_starvation") | not))
    | map(.value)
    | map(select(type == "object"))
    | map(select(.driver == "flow:auto_codex"))') || {
    echo "RETIREMENT: unknown - the roster did not parse"; exit 3; }

# LIVENESS IS A FOUR-VALUE VOCABULARY: live, released, stale, unknown. Only the
# middle two are conclusively inactive. A role whose liveness is `unknown` - the
# registry could not determine whether the process exists - is NOT evidence of
# absence, and counting it as such would authorise deleting the command out from
# under a session that is still running on it.
live=$(printf '%s' "$roster"    | jq -r '[ .[] | select(.liveness == "live") ] | length')
undet=$(printf '%s' "$roster"   | jq -r '[ .[] | select(.liveness == "unknown") ] | length')

if   [ "$live"  != "0" ]; then echo "RETIREMENT: blocked ($live live in $WAVE)"
elif [ "$undet" != "0" ]; then echo "RETIREMENT: unknown ($undet role(s) of undetermined liveness in $WAVE)"
else                           echo "RETIREMENT: clear for $WAVE"
fi
```

**There is no verb that enumerates waves** (`register|policy|list|get|verify|
release|self-address`), so this is per-wave by construction and the caller
supplies `$WAVE`. A wave nobody thought to check is not evidence of absence -
which is the whole reason the third outcome exists.

Three outcomes, never two: `clear`, `blocked`, `unknown`. **`unknown` is not
`clear`.** That is the same rule this repository applies to every other
instrument, spelled out here because the tempting one-line grep silently
collapses all three into "no output, go ahead" - and because the first draft of
this very check did exactly that, then was replaced by a `jq` expression written
against a registry shape that does not exist, which would have returned `0`
forever and authorised the deletion unconditionally.

While the condition does not hold, this file stays and the retirement is a
residual rather than an oversight - recorded here beside the thing it governs,
not in a merged PR body the next person will not read.

The trigger is deliberately about LIVE ROLES rather than a date. A deadline
would expire while someone was mid-run; this cannot.

## Closing report

<!-- closing-report-surface -->

This command ends a run - by delegating it - so it owes the owner the same
closing report the lifecycle drivers do. **Follow
[the closing-report contract](docs/agents/closing-report-contract.md)** -
canonical there, not restated here.

Delegation does not move the obligation. A reader who typed `/flow-auto_codex`
gets their report from this run, whatever command executed the steps; a
"see the other command" pointer would be an omission wearing a redirect.

Three sections, in this order:

1. `## TO-DO (owner)` - FIRST and always present. Numbered; each item names the
   DECISION, not its background. `Nothing blocking.` stated explicitly when
   there is nothing, because an omitted block reads as forgotten rather than as
   none. An FYI is not a TO-DO.
2. `## In plain language` - what was wrong, why it mattered, what is better now,
   under `/flow-eli5` Section A's existing depth floor.
3. `## Evidence` - quality-gate output, the counter-model receipt path and its
   counts, the security scan verdict, the commit and push results, the PR URL,
   and any nit-store comment links. Demoted, never deleted.
